steps.content: 36 hours before the hearing, 4:29 A.M.
You've just wrapped up the day's work, ready to get some rest, but a source of bright light draws you to the second floor of the workspace.
The light comes from your office. You let Matilda use the office, where she has easy access to a large amount of documents and confidential information.
There haven't been many pressing matters that require your attention lately. To give Matilda space, you moved out of your office. Nevertheless, you're surprised to find Matilda up this late.
The door is ajar. You ease it open wider. Behind the mountain of files and disposable coffee cups on the table, you see the person hard at work.
The soft rustling of pen against paper is constant in the quiet, and she doesn't seem to notice your presence.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: Chief?

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: You're still up?

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Just got off work.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Are you still prepping for tomorrow's hearing?

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: ...Yes.
Matilda sounds tired. Still, she's making an effort to keep lethargy out of her voice while answering you.

You glance at the corner of the table and notice the sheets of paper covered with color-coded notes. From something as small as a punctuation mark to something as large as a whole paragraph, nothing has escaped her meticulous pen. Collectively, they reflect the writer's thorough thought process.
However, it's obvious that this stack of paper is unwanted.
The writer holds herself to extremely high standards, and while that is true, it's the mental burden that plays a major role in her being so hard on herself.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Only a few pages of paper...

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: Sorry, what did you say?
Your voice is low, and Matilda has a lapse of concentration and fails to catch what you've just said.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: What I was trying to say is, we've been through a lot in the West District, but it can be summed up on just a few pieces of copy paper.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: It's in fact a story worthy of the adjective "epic."
You remove a piece of paper from the unwanted stack and give it a quick scan.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: A lot of numbers in here, a lot of zeros. Like how much drinking water the West District needs every day, or how many emergency supplies, or how much of this or that is needed to maintain the stability of the entire West District.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: You must've put a lot of thought into deciding on what units to use; you're trying to explain the problems faced by the West District without embarrassing the people involved too much.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Unfortunately, numbers are cold. They arise from the collision of different interests; they are conditions added as an afterthought when the big shots are trying to reach an agreement.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Even the experiences we had together in the West District, the emotions these experiences evoked... They can tell a more touching tale than numbers ever will.
Matilda listens to your long speech. When you're finished, she puts down the pen she's holding.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: How I wish I could tell stories to them.
Matilda rises to her feet, reaches out reflexively for a paper cup, but catches herself.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: At this hour... I don't think it's a good idea to offer you coffee.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: It's okay. Take a break. Let's have a chat.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Speaking of stories, I know nothing about your story before you joined the Executive Committee. Care to share it?
Matilda looks you in the eye, and sighs as if with resignation.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: Are you always this blunt when you "chat" with others?

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Haha...
Matilda looks away from your smiling face and toward the window.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: My story is not a complicated one... My childhood was not that different from that of most Eastside children. If there's any difference, it's probably that my father's last name is Cavendish.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: I grew up under the protection of my parents. Until the incident in N.F. 104 changed everything...

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: Yes.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: The political scene of Eastside was thrown into turmoil that year. That came about when Abel, a candidate for the Speaker's seat supported by the Cavendish family, was assassinated and died during a campaign speech.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: The Cavendish family poured all its resources into this attempt at ascending to the peak of power in the City Council, but almost ended up the way the Executive Committee did, narrowly avoiding the fate of being divided up by the family's political enemies.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: My parents lost their lives in the turmoil...

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: ...It must have been a very difficult time.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: For the family, yes.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: But relatively speaking, I was lucky...

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: After my parents passed away, my aunt, Ms. Bernadette, adopted me.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Your guardian is the star councilor in the City Council, the leader of a political family... She couldn't have had much time for her small "family," right?
Matilda gives a soft laugh, her eyes sparkling.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: You're right. She didn't have much time to care for me. But that doesn't mean she failed as a guardian.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: She sent me to the best elite school in all of Eastside, hired the best teachers to give me private lessons on etiquette and teach me all the other skills useful in social situations...

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: We didn't spend much time together, but whenever she was with me, she'd always let me know that she knew about my latest achievements, and she'd give me suggestions for what I should do next.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: I made many mistakes, but she never made me feel bad about them.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: She allowed my mistakes, my immaturity, my shortsightedness.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: At the same time, she made a point of telling me, "The most important thing is to find your true self when your mistakes lead you astray and locate the path that suits you best."

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Find your true self, huh? Sounds like your aunt was a major influence in your life.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Sadly, your aunt's true self seems to have led her to a completely different path from yours.
Matilda's bright eyes dull somewhat at your remark.
She closes her eyes, as if reminiscing, or contemplating the true meaning of the term "true self."
After a long while, she opens her eyes and, slowly, she speaks:

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: I didn't understand what true self really meant at first.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: I was just an ordinary person, with no outstanding talents. I couldn't hold a candle to those real geniuses at the elite school.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: From the textbooks, the teachers at the school, the propaganda from Eastside... I learned the rules of society.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: I thought that if I followed these rules and worked really hard, I could at least narrow the gap between Ms. Bernadette and me.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: It's like target practice... Do you know anything about target practice, Chief?

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: The concept of target practice is simple. All you need to do is hit the bull's-eye, or get as close to it as you can.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: For the longest time, I stayed in the shooting range that was Eastside and shot targets other people put up for me...

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: Ms. Bernadette, taught me all the techniques and rules, and even the "gun" in my hand was given by her.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: I used to think that I didn't need to think too much, that all I needed to do was shoot the targets, but now...

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: I don't know when, but my target has changed, and the person who has been standing behind me and supporting me is now blocking my view of the bull's-eye I want so much to hit.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: And you can't bring yourself to pull the trigger this time around?

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: I wouldn't dare.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: Forgive me, I'm just too immature.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: I don't think this is a matter of maturity.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: You're just worried, about how that relative who means so much to you will treat you after your bullet hits the bull's-eye.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: You're worried that there will no be turning back once you pull the trigger, right?
Matilda is silent for a long while, then nods with resignation.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: But isn't your true self telling you to aim for this particular bull's-eye?

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: "The most important thing is to find your true self when your mistakes lead you astray and locate the path that suits you best."
Doubt is leaving Matilda's eyes.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: You're right, Chief. I...

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: I get it now. Instead of being timid, I should just pull the trigger first.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Not my words. That's what Ms. Bernadette taught you, isn't it?

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: You're right.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: You have a great aunt.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Sensible, wise, patient with her descendants, and willing to guide.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Among the many Sinners in the MBCC, very few can claim to have a relative half as good as yours.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Maybe she's just been deceived by the one-sided voices in Eastside?

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Tomorrow, at the hearing, when you go up there to speak the truth about the West District and awe everyone present, I believe she'll understand why you do what you do.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: The people of the West District have changed you. I can't see why they can't change more people. Have faith in Ms. Bernadette.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: If you win over a powerful ally like your aunt, the future of the West District will be even more secure.
Matilda looks out of the window.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: Perhaps...
Sensing Matilda's reluctance to talk more about her aunt, you drop the subject.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: In any case, don't stress yourself out. Just go do what you want to do and what you should do. I'll support you in the background.
Matilda turns her gaze toward you. The smile she gives you this time is filled with warmth and determination.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: Mm... I know.
She thinks for a moment, then speaks again:

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: Thank you for taking the time to chat with me about these things.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: I won't let you guys down.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: You're welcome...
You yawn, feeling sleepy.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Go to bed as soon as you finish revising the draft. You don't want to speak at the hearing with dark circles under your eyes.
Matilda smiles and nods.

steps.speaker: Matilda
steps.content: Mm, you should get some rest too.
